name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley Superstore out by the motorway junction, the big one with forty aisles and a car park you could land a plane on. I'm the senior on the customer service desk and the returns counter, and I cover the staffed tills at weekends. I start at nine, open the desk, sort out refunds, deal with lost cards and answer the phone when somebody can't find their trolley token. It's steady and I'm good at it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody needs to explain anything to me, I know the layout, the managers and which customers will argue. What wears me out is the complaints, about eight a day, and the fact that half the shop is now self-checkout so the people who come to me are already annoyed. AI? No, I don't touch it. My phone has a calculator and a camera and that's enough. My girlfriend Nadia, who's a teaching assistant at a primary school, says I'm stubborn. I say I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. At work I'd tell the younger lads there's no need to jump at every new gadget. To friends I'd say it was the same with the internet and the mobile phone, a lot of fuss and then life carried on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on, mostly. But Hartley's already struggling against the discount chains, so I'm not that relaxed. There was a round of cuts last winter, two people from the back office, and the rumour is the desk could get merged with the tills next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my hours and my pay, and I'd keep saving, we've got about nine months in the bank between Nadia and me. I wouldn't change anything. If Hartley's keeps shrinking I'd look at the supermarkets on the ring road, there are plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, I suppose. A bit uneasy because of Hartley's, not because of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the rumours of the desk being merged.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the store manager, Kevin, said they're reviewing the layout. That's manager talk for fewer people. If the desk goes I'd move to the tills or the deli, and honestly I'd be okay, but I don't want to go backwards in my role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the discount chains really worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The discount chains worry me more than robots, because every quarter head office says the numbers need to improve. They've taken customers off us for two years, to be honest. I'd rather work for a busy shop than a quiet one.

say: I'd tell younger colleagues there's no need to jump at every new **gadget**.
I'd tell friends it's like the **internet** and the phone: fuss, then life carried on.
think: Hartley's is **struggling** against the discount chains, and there were cuts last winter.
The rumour is my **desk** could be merged with the tills.
do: Keep my **hours** and keep saving with Nadia.
Move to the **tills** or deli if the desk is merged.
Look at the other **supermarkets** on the ring road if Hartley's shrinks.
feel: **Uneasy** because of Hartley's, not because of AI.
S0.quote: The discount chains worry me more than robots, because every quarter head office says the numbers need to improve.
fieldNote: His unease comes from an old **pressure**, a shop losing ground to discounters, so calm would not fit.
He shrugs at AI but cares about **holding** his own role.

steps.text: Keep the desk shifts and save with Nadia
Put three hundred a month aside while the layout review runs
Wait to see whether Hartley's merges the desk and tills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was bound to happen and people should get on with it. At work I'd say, show me the proof first, because I've seen head office buy things that don't work. To friends I'd say the shops will use it for ordering and for answering emails, not for talking to a customer who's lost their receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means less than it sounds for the floor, but plenty for the desk. A chatbot can do the phone and the refund form, and half my desk job is those two. They'll say it frees me up for the real customer, then cut one desk shift out of three. That's where I think I'm exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, but properly, and make myself the person who handles the awkward cases that a machine can't. I'd ask Kevin to put me on the exceptions and complaints. I'd save a bit more, maybe four hundred a month, and ask the union rep about what's in our contracts. I'd still avoid the AI tools if I can get away with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, to be honest. It's not about being scared of machines, it's about my particular job being easy to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd avoid the tools. Does that make you more exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Nadia says so. But I don't see the point of learning something that I think will be used to replace me. If they make me use it, I'll learn it, and I'd rather do that than chase it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Hartley's cut your desk shift to three days a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the Saturday tills shift and look at a second part-time job. And I'd be angry, quietly. I'd never throw a fit in the store, I'd just start sending out my CV the same night.

say: I'd say it was bound to happen, but **show me** the proof first.
I'd tell friends shops will use it for **ordering** and emails, not for an upset customer.
think: A chatbot can handle the **phone** and refund forms, which are half my desk job.
They'll say it frees me up, then cut a **desk shift** out of three.
do: Ask Kevin to put me on **complaints** and awkward cases a machine can't do.
Save about four hundred a month and ask the **union** rep about my contract.
Take Saturday **tills** shifts if my desk hours drop.
feel: **Worried**, because my particular job is easy to copy.
S1.quote: I don't see the point of learning something that I think will be used to replace me.
fieldNote: **Resistance** to the tools leaves him more exposed than steadier colleagues, and he half knows it.
He would send out his CV the same night hours are cut, which shows more **resolve** than his calm voice suggests.

steps.text: Ask Kevin to put me on complaints and exception cases
Ask the union rep what the contract says about hours
Take Saturday tills shifts if desk hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too fast, and nobody asked me. At work I'd say let's wait and see what the company does. To friends I'd say I don't believe it'll be that quick, and I'd mean it half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's real, the desk goes first because it's all answering and refunds, and then the tills around 2031. That's both parts of my job. I'd feel it in my gut that I'm in the wrong line of work, and I'm not a person who changes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare penny into savings and cut the car payments and the streaming. I'd talk to Nadia about us moving in with her sister to save rent for a while. I'd look at a trade, maybe forklift or warehouse maintenance, something at the back of a supermarket that robots will still need people for. And I'd go to the union meeting for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A real knot. I'd keep telling myself I have savings and Nadia's job is secure, because that's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nadia's job is secure. Does that change how worried you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. She earns less than me but it's a school and they don't replace teaching assistants with a machine overnight. If it were just me I'd be a lot more scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade and not an AI course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm a hands-on person. If I'm going to learn something new I'd rather learn it with a spanner than a screen. And the warehouse supervisor at Hartley's said they always need maintenance people.

say: I'd say it's too much, too fast, and **nobody** asked me.
At work I'd say let's **wait** and see what the company does.
think: The **desk** goes first, then the tills around 2031, which is both parts of my job.
I'm not a person who changes **fast**, and that scares me.
do: Put every spare penny into **savings** and cut the car payments and streaming.
Learn a **trade**, such as warehouse maintenance, that robots still need people for.
Go to the **union** meeting for the first time.
feel: **Anxious**, a real knot, softened by savings and Nadia's secure job.
S2.quote: If I'm going to learn something new I'd rather learn it with a spanner than a screen.
fieldNote: He is **anxious** rather than alarmed because his partner's school job and nine months of savings hold him up.
He **prefers** retraining on tools over screens, which matches his resistance to AI.

steps.text: Move every spare penny into savings
Start a warehouse maintenance course in the evenings
Go to the union meeting for the first time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for people to adapt, but they won't. At work I'd keep my head down and watch. Online I wouldn't say anything, I'm not that sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have some breathing room. The desk probably changes around 2031 and the tills around 2034, so I've got time, but I know my habit is to wait until it's urgent. That's what Nadia worries about, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to learn one trade skill, probably forklift and a basic maintenance certificate, evenings and Sundays. I'd stay at Hartley's and keep saving about five hundred a month. And I'd try the AI tool at the desk once, just once, to see if it's as bad as I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less. Five years feels like I could do something about it, if I did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, and not wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia putting the course form in front of me, honestly. She'd do it. And maybe if Hartley's cut one person from the desk, then I'd see it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cashier at Hartley's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't be like me and wait until it's urgent, learn the new bit while you're young and keep a few months of rent saved. That's the real protection.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to adapt, but most people **won't**.
I'd keep my head down and **watch**, not post online.
think: I've got some **breathing room**, but my habit is to wait until it's urgent.
The desk changes around 2031 and the **tills** around 2034.
do: Do a forklift and maintenance **certificate** on evenings and Sundays.
Keep saving about five hundred a month at **Hartley's**.
Try the desk's AI tool **once** to see if it's as bad as I think.
feel: **Anxious**, but less, because five years gives me something to act on.
S3.quote: Don't be like me and wait until it's urgent, learn the new bit while you're young and keep a few months of rent saved.
fieldNote: Time **softens** his mood but does not fix his habit of waiting, and he knows it.
He is **willing** to try the AI tool once, which is more than in any other scenario.

steps.text: Take a forklift and maintenance certificate on evenings and Sundays
Save five hundred a month while staying at Hartley's
Try the desk's AI tool once
Keep working the desk and weekend tills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a lot of time and a lot can change in ten years. At work I'd say nothing, it's too far off. To friends, I'd tell them we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it's the easiest to ignore, and that's a risk. By 2036 I'd be 37, and I'd like to be a supervisor by then, so it fits my plans anyway. The robots only come in 2039, which feels like another life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my way up at Hartley's and try for desk supervisor in two or three years. I'd save for a house deposit with Nadia, and I'd learn the tools only when the company makes me. I'd probably still be stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit calm, a bit uneasy, because I know I'm the type to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house with a ten-year warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but a small one, with a mortgage I can carry on a single wage if I had to. Nadia and I would want about a third of it saved first. It's the sensible way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says AI is overhyped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they might be right. But being wrong costs a lot more than saving a bit extra, so I'd hedge even if AI turns out to be overhyped.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can **change**.
I'd tell friends we'll **see**, and say nothing at work.
think: It's the easiest to **ignore**, and that is a risk.
By 2036 I'd like to be a **supervisor**, so it fits my plans anyway.
do: Aim for desk **supervisor** at Hartley's in two or three years.
Save a third of a **house** deposit with Nadia.
Learn the **tools** only when the company makes me.
feel: **Uneasy**, partly calm, because I know I put things off.
S4.quote: Being wrong costs a lot more than saving a bit extra, so I'd hedge even if AI turns out to be overhyped.
fieldNote: Ten years makes it easy to look away, and he knows that is his weak spot.
His one firm idea is to hedge with **savings** and a house he could carry on one wage.

steps.text: Aim for desk supervisor at Hartley's in two or three years
Save a third of a house deposit with Nadia
Buy a small house we could carry on one wage
Learn new tools only when the company requires it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm the sort who needs time to move, and I'd have none. What would help is the company telling us early what it plans to do, a proper notice period and some paid training for hands-on jobs. And a bit of honesty from Hartley's about which jobs are going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People assume I don't care because I stay quiet, but I know exactly which customers will argue and which ones just need five minutes. I do care. I just don't see the point of getting excited about something until I know what it does to the desk, the tills and the people I work beside.

headlineQuote: People assume I don't care because I stay quiet, but I know exactly which customers will argue and which ones just need five minutes.
portrait: **Erik** is a 27-year-old senior on the customer service desk at Hartley Superstore, a big out-of-town supermarket.
He is centre politically and **resistant** to new technology, and has never used AI.
His worry is concrete: the desk's phone and refund work looks **easy to copy**, and Hartley's is already shrinking.
He has about nine months saved and a partner with a secure job, so his mood sits around **anxious** more than alarmed.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because he needs time to change and would have none.
whatWouldHelp: Early **notice** from Hartley's, a proper notice period and paid training for hands-on jobs.
